name: Product catalog search
summary: One search box that must serve both a pasted product id and a vague sentence, on the OpenSearch cluster the retailer already runs.

brief.whoIsAsking: A shopper who types 'blue waterproof jacket under 120' or pastes a product id from a receipt, expecting both to work in the same box.
brief.whatTheyNeedBack: The product id hits exactly on a keyword; the sentence finds the jacket even when the wording does not match the title; the wrong-region sku never appears.
brief.systemsAlreadyRunning: A few million SKUs in OpenSearch, already the keyword search cluster. The search team keeps running it and will not adopt a second store. Prices and availability change through the day on a product bus.
brief.breaksWhen: The receipt lookup stops working. A shopper pasting a product id is the highest-intent traffic on the site, and a search box that fails them is worse than having added no semantic search at all.
brief.doneMeans: The product id still hits on a keyword, the sentence finds the jacket even when the wording does not match the title, the EU-only sku is filtered out before ranking, and a guide unpublished this morning is gone from the index tonight.

steps.title: Hybrid search, because the id is a keyword
steps.decision: Whether the box is a vector search, or a hybrid of keyword and vector, so a pasted product id and a vague sentence both work.
steps.why: A product id from a receipt is an exact token: it either matches or it does not, and a keyword (BM25) search nails it. A vague sentence shares no words with the title and needs a vector search. A vector-only store answers the sentence and fails the id — the id embeds to a point near nothing, and the highest-intent traffic on the site gets zero results. That is the Breaks when exactly. Hybrid runs both and fuses the scores (on Bedrock, overrideSearchType HYBRID on a knowledge base whose store is the existing OpenSearch cluster), so the id hits on the keyword side and the sentence hits on the vector side. This is runnable: the hybrid query returns the jacket for the sentence and the exact sku for the id. The losing choice is vector-only, which quietly breaks the receipt lookup.

snippets.label: The Retrieve client. A Bedrock knowledge base over the OpenSearch cluster the retailer already runs.
snippets.source:
import boto3

agent = boto3.client("bedrock-agent-runtime", region_name="eu-central-1")

KB_ID = "CATALOG123"  # the knowledge base whose store is the existing OpenSearch domain
QUERY = "blue waterproof jacket under 120"

snippets.label: Ask for a hybrid search: keyword and vector, fused. The id matches on the keyword side; the sentence matches on the vector side.
From the terminal, confirm the knowledge base is ACTIVE and see its store — get-knowledge-base before you debug the query.

files.body:
# Assemble the hybrid query from the snippets on the left, then Run. The
# intercept returns the jacket for the sentence.
#
# The goal: one query with a keyword clause and a vector clause, so the id
# and the sentence both work in the same box.

With a knowledge base on OpenSearch, overrideSearchType HYBRID asks the
store to fuse BM25 and kNN scores; the normalization the fusion needs is
configured by the service and the search team's cluster. The lesson is the
shape: two clauses, two retrieval mechanisms, one result list. A vector-only
store (next step's refusal) cannot express the keyword clause at all, which
is why it fails the id.

steps.title: S3 Vectors is refused here
steps.decision: Whether to move to S3 Vectors, the store you would pick with no hybrid need and no cluster to run, or keep the OpenSearch cluster that is already there.
steps.why: S3 Vectors is genuinely the right default for a greenfield vector workload: no cluster to operate, cheap at rest, managed. But it has no keyword side, and this catalog has two hard requirements it cannot meet — a hybrid of keyword and vector, and an existing OpenSearch cluster the search team keeps running. Choosing S3 Vectors here means re-adding keyword search on top of a store that has none, and abandoning a cluster that already works. The store is refused not because it is bad but because the requirements rule it out. Configuration: the lesson is naming when S3 Vectors wins and why it loses here.

snippets.label: What S3 Vectors is for — and the note that this catalog's hybrid requirement rules it out.

files.body:
This is the mirror of the policy assistant's 'managed knowledge base' step,
which chose the managed default. Here the managed default (S3 Vectors) is
refused, and the reasoning is symmetric: pick the store the requirements
fit, not the store that is fashionable. The hybrid requirement is the
disqualifier — S3 Vectors has no BM25 side — and the existing cluster is
the second. Either alone would be enough.

checks.message: The store stays OpenSearch: it has the keyword side the product id needs and it is already running.
The reasoning is recorded: a store with no keyword side fails the receipt lookup, the Breaks when.
S3 Vectors is not selected as the store. It is the right default for a greenfield vector-only workload, not for a hybrid catalog on an existing cluster.

steps.title: Two chunk shapes for two document shapes
steps.decision: Whether one chunking rule covers both the short spec sheets and the long buying guides, or each shape gets its own.
steps.why: A product page is a short spec sheet; a buying guide is long prose. One chunking rule cannot serve both: fixed-size small enough for the spec sheet shreds the guide into fragments that lose the argument, and semantic chunking sized for the guide swallows a whole spec sheet into one undifferentiated blob. So the ingest branches on document type — fixed-size on the product pages, semantic on the guides. Configuration: the lesson is chunking by document shape, decided at ingest. The losing choice is one global rule applied to everything, which quietly degrades whichever shape it was not tuned for.

snippets.label: Branch the chunking on document type: fixed-size for spec sheets, semantic for guides.

files.body:
Chunking is a per-shape decision far more often than teams treat it. The
policy assistant used one strategy because its corpus was one shape
(policies). This catalog is two shapes with opposite needs, so the ingest
branches. The symptom of getting it wrong is shape-specific: guides that
retrieve as disconnected fragments (fixed-size too small) or spec sheets
where every query returns the same giant blob (semantic too large).

checks.message: Semantic chunking on the long guides keeps an argument together across paragraphs.
Fixed-size chunking on the short spec sheets keeps a fact retrievable without a whole sheet collapsing into one chunk.
The strategy branches on document type at ingest, so each shape gets the chunking it needs rather than one global rule.

steps.title: Rerank for the item in third place
steps.decision: What to do when the right item is in the result list but ranked third — swap the embedding model, or rerank the candidates.
steps.why: The jacket is already retrieved; it is just in third place behind two near-matches. That is not an embedding problem — the retrieval found it — so swapping the embedding model is the wrong fix, an expensive rebuild that does not address ranking. A reranker (a cross-encoder like Cohere Rerank on Bedrock) takes the top candidates and the query together and reorders them by relevance, promoting the jacket to first. This is runnable: the rerank call reorders the candidates and the jacket comes first. The losing move is treating third-place as a retrieval failure and rebuilding the index, when the retrieval already succeeded.

snippets.label: The candidates from the first-pass search, in the wrong order. The right jacket is third.
snippets.source:
import boto3, json

bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="eu-central-1")

QUERY = "blue waterproof jacket under 120"
candidates = [
    "Navy rain poncho, one size",
    "Blue windbreaker, not waterproof",
    "Coastline Waterproof Shell Jacket, blue",  # the right one, third
]

snippets.label: Rerank the candidates against the query. A cross-encoder scores query+doc together, so the jacket moves to first.
snippets.source:
out = bedrock.invoke_model(
    modelId="cohere.rerank-v3-5:0",
    body=json.dumps({"api_version": 2, "query": QUERY, "documents": candidates, "top_n": 3}),
)
ranked = json.loads(out["body"].read())
print("rerank request", ranked["id"])
for r in ranked["results"]:
    print(r["index"], r["relevance_score"], candidates[r["index"]])

snippets.label: From the terminal, confirm the rerank model is available in the Region before wiring it in — a model not enabled is an access error, not a bad call.

files.body:
# Assemble the rerank call from the snippets on the left, then Run. The
# intercept returns the candidates reordered, the jacket first.
#
# The goal: reorder candidates that were already retrieved, rather than
# rebuilding the index for a ranking problem.

The distinction is retrieval vs ranking. Retrieval decides which documents
are candidates; ranking decides their order. Third place means retrieval
succeeded and ranking is weak — a reranker fixes ranking directly. A new
embedding model changes which documents are candidates, which is a fix for
a recall problem (the right item not retrieved at all), not a precision-at-1
problem. Reaching for a re-embed here is expensive and off-target.

steps.title: Rewrite the vague query, HyDE the alien one
steps.decision: What to do with a question that shares no words with the catalog — rewrite it toward catalog vocabulary, or generate a hypothetical document to search with.
steps.why: 'Something for a wet commute that packs small' names no product and shares no words with any title. Two tools, two situations. Query rewrite rephrases the question into catalog vocabulary ('lightweight packable waterproof jacket') so the keyword side has something to match. HyDE goes further for a question that looks nothing like any title: the model writes a hypothetical product description answering the question, and you search with that document's embedding, because a fake answer is closer to the real answer than the question is. This is runnable: the rewrite returns catalog words. The losing move is searching the raw vague sentence and returning noise.

snippets.label: Rewrite the vague question into catalog vocabulary, so the keyword clause has words to match.
snippets.source:
import boto3, json

bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="eu-central-1")

VAGUE = "something for a wet commute that packs small"
rewrite = bedrock.converse(
    modelId="eu.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": f"Rewrite as catalog search terms: {VAGUE}"}]}],
    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 64},
)
terms = rewrite["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"]
print(terms)

snippets.label: From the terminal, list the models so you confirm the Converse model id is one you can call in this Region.

files.body:
# Assemble the query rewrite from the snippet on the left, then Run. The
# intercept returns catalog-vocabulary search terms.
#
# The goal: turn a vague sentence into words the catalog actually uses,
# before it reaches the search.

Rewrite and HyDE are a ladder. Rewrite is cheap and enough when the
question is just phrased in everyday words — map 'wet commute' to
'waterproof, packable.' HyDE is for the question that resembles no title at
all: generate a fake ideal product page, embed THAT, and search. The
tradeoff is a model call on the query path, so it is reserved for the vague
tail, not every search. An exact product id never goes near either — it
goes straight to the keyword clause.

steps.title: Deduplicate the near-copy seller pages
steps.decision: Whether five near-identical seller descriptions all go into the prompt, or they are collapsed to one before ranking.
steps.why: Marketplace sellers paste near-copies of the same description. Five identical-ish pages are not five pieces of evidence — they are one, repeated, and if they all fill the context they crowd out the genuinely different results and bias the model toward the duplicated claim. Dedup collapses near-copies before they reach the prompt, by a similarity threshold on the candidate embeddings or a shingled-text hash, keeping one representative. Configuration: the lesson is dedup before the prompt. The losing choice is letting the top-k be five copies of one listing, which wastes the context window and misleads the ranking.

snippets.label: Collapse near-duplicate candidates before they fill the prompt. Keep one representative per cluster.

files.body:
Dedup sits between retrieval and the prompt, a cheap but easily-skipped
stage. The threshold is a judgment: too high and genuine variants of a real
product line get collapsed; too low and near-copies slip through. Shingled
text hashing is the cheaper first pass; embedding-cosine catches
reworded-but-identical listings the hash misses. The cost of skipping it is
a context window full of the same claim five times.

checks.message: Near-copies are collapsed by a similarity threshold, so five pasted variants become one piece of evidence.
Dedup runs on the candidates before the prompt, keeping one representative per near-duplicate cluster.
One representative per near-duplicate cluster reaches the prompt, so duplicates do not crowd out genuinely different results or bias the ranking.

steps.title: Event-driven ingest from the product bus
steps.decision: Whether the index is rebuilt on a schedule, or updated by events from the product bus as prices and stock change.
steps.why: Prices and availability change through the day on the product bus. A nightly rebuild serves this morning's discontinued sku until tonight — a shopper is offered something that is gone. Event-driven ingest subscribes to the bus: a product update event updates that document, a discontinue event removes it, within minutes. The index tracks the catalog instead of lagging a day behind it. Configuration: the lesson is the event subscription, not the cron. The losing choice is the scheduled rebuild, which guarantees a window where the index and the catalog disagree — and a guide unpublished this morning must be gone tonight (Done means), which a daily job cannot promise.

snippets.label: Subscribe the ingest to the product bus. An update event updates the doc; a discontinue event removes it.

files.body:
Same event-driven-vs-scheduled decision as the policy assistant's ingest
step, with a retail urgency: stock and price move intraday, so the lag of a
nightly job is customer-visible (an out-of-stock result) rather than merely
stale. ProductDiscontinued must delete the vectors, not just stop updating
them — a retained vector keeps a dead sku retrievable, the same
stale-answer failure in a catalog.

checks.message: A product-updated event reindexes the document, so a price or stock change is reflected within minutes.
A discontinue event removes the document, so a dead sku leaves the index rather than lingering until a rebuild.
The ingest subscribes to the product bus, so the index tracks the catalog event-by-event instead of lagging a nightly job.

steps.title: Filter the store region before similarity
steps.decision: Whether the store-region filter runs before the similarity search or after, so a US shopper is never offered an EU-only sku.
steps.why: A shopper in the US store must not be offered an EU-only sku, however well it matches. The region filter runs before ranking: the kNN and keyword clauses search only documents whose store region includes the shopper's store, so the EU-only sku is never a candidate. Filter after and the EU sku was retrieved, scored, and is one display bug away from being shown. Closeness does not override which store the shopper is in. Configuration: the lesson is the pre-filter on store region. The losing choice is a post-filter that trusts the result list to be scrubbed before display.

snippets.label: The region filter is a clause in the query, ANDed with the hybrid search. The EU-only sku is not a candidate.

files.body:
Same 'filter before similarity' discipline as the policy assistant's
department filter and the contract desk's client filter — a recurring exam
pattern. In OpenSearch the filter clause of a bool query restricts the set
the must clauses score, so it is genuinely pre-scoring, not a re-rank. The
store_region field has to be on every document, or a missing value drops a
valid sku silently, the same missing-key trap as the policy sidecar.

checks.message: The store-region filter restricts candidates to the shopper's store before scoring, so an EU-only sku is never retrieved for a US shopper.
The region is a bool filter clause, which OpenSearch applies before the must clauses score — genuinely pre-similarity, not a re-rank.
No post_filter scrubbing the result list. A post-filter means the EU sku was retrieved and scored, one display bug away from being shown.

steps.title: overrideSearchType only on a store that has keyword
steps.decision: Whether overrideSearchType is a flag you can set anywhere, or one that only means something on a store with a keyword side.
steps.why: overrideSearchType=HYBRID tells the Retrieve API to run both the keyword and vector sides and fuse them. It is meaningful here precisely because OpenSearch has a keyword side to override toward. On a store with no keyword mechanism — S3 Vectors, a pure vector index — the flag has nothing to switch to: there is no BM25 pass to combine, so setting it is either ignored or an error, and a reviewer who copied it from a hybrid example is cargo-culting. Configuration: the lesson is that the flag is a property of the store's capability, not a universal switch. The losing move is pasting overrideSearchType onto a vector-only store and expecting hybrid behavior that the store cannot provide.

snippets.label: overrideSearchType is set because this store supports hybrid. It is not a flag you paste onto a vector-only store.

files.body:
This step closes the loop with step 3's refusal of S3 Vectors: the same
capability gap (no keyword side) that disqualified the store also makes
this flag meaningless there. The flag is a knowledge-base Retrieve setting;
it presumes the underlying store can do both retrievals. Recognizing that a
configuration option is a function of the store's capabilities, not a free
switch, is the transferable lesson.

checks.message: overrideSearchType HYBRID is set because OpenSearch has a keyword side to fuse with the vector side.
The flag is justified by the store's capability. It is meaningful here because there is a keyword pass to override toward.
On a vector-only store the flag has nothing to switch to. It is store-dependent, not a universal switch pasted from a hybrid example.
